title: CDN Architecture
description: Explore how Content Delivery Networks make the web faster by moving data closer to users.

data.text: A Content Delivery Network, or CDN, is a globally distributed network of servers that cache and deliver web content from locations close to users. Instead of every request traveling across continents to a single origin server, a CDN serves a cached copy from a nearby edge node. The result is lower latency, faster page loads, and reduced load on the origin.

CDNs were invented in the late 1990s to solve a simple physics problem: the speed of light is finite. A user in Tokyo and a user in New York accessing the same server in San Francisco experience very different round-trip times. By caching content at dozens or hundreds of locations worldwide, CDNs shrink that distance.

When a browser requests a resource, the DNS resolution usually routes the request to the nearest CDN edge server. If the edge server already has a fresh cached copy, it returns the file immediately. If not, it fetches the content from the origin server, caches it, and then delivers it to the user.

data.caption: How a CDN edge server sits between the user and the origin.
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    U[User] -->|Request| EDGE[CDN Edge Node]
    EDGE -->|Cache Hit| U
    EDGE -->|Cache Miss| ORIGIN[Origin Server]
    ORIGIN -->|Response| EDGE
    EDGE -->|Cache + Serve| U

data.title: Core CDN Components
items: Edge servers — data centers in major cities that cache content close to users.
Origin server — the original source of content, such as your application server or object storage.
DNS routing — GeoDNS or Anycast directs users to the optimal edge node.
Cache hierarchy — a layered cache that can include regional and parent nodes before reaching the origin.
Purge and invalidation — mechanisms to remove stale content when the source changes.

data.text: CDNs use cache-control headers, expiration rules, and content hashing to decide what to store and for how long. Static assets like images, CSS, and JavaScript are ideal candidates because they change infrequently and benefit from aggressive caching. Dynamic content requires more careful configuration to avoid serving stale personalized data.

terms.definition: A CDN server located close to end users, responsible for serving cached content and reducing origin load.
The percentage of requests served from cache. Higher ratios mean better performance and lower origin costs.
A routing technique where many servers share the same IP address. DNS or BGP directs users to the nearest server.

data.title: Watch Out for Stale Content
data.text: A high cache hit ratio is great for speed, but it can serve outdated content after a deployment. Always plan invalidation for critical assets and use versioned filenames with content hashes for static files.

data.title: Cache-Control Header Example
data.content: Set aggressive caching for static assets and no-cache for sensitive HTML.
data.code:
# For static assets with content hash
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# For sensitive HTML pages
Cache-Control: private, no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CDNs cache content at edge servers worldwide to reduce latency and origin load.
DNS routing and caching headers determine which content is cached and for how long.
Static assets benefit from aggressive caching, while dynamic content needs careful invalidation.
Modern CDNs often include WAF, DDoS protection, and image optimization as built-in features.
data.takeaway: A well-configured CDN is one of the highest-impact optimizations you can make for a global web application.
